The Taos Avalanche Center reported widespread avalanche activity in the backcountry across the northern Sangre de Cristo Mountains on March 10th. Weak layers deep down in the snowpack could not support the weight of the 10 to 20 inches of heavy snow that fell with this winter storm along with additional heavy snow that had fallen in the week prior. These avalanches that occurred were hundreds of feet wide and about 3 to 5 feet thick and ran well into the trees that were over 1,000 feet below. While nobody was hurt, there was one close call when a skier was pushed over in steep terrain and was buried in a tree well for several minutes. Fortunately, their friends were able to dig them out. An Avalanche Warning that was in effect for the area kept other traffic low in the backcountry during this storm. The only damages done were to trees.

The combination of snow and high winds in Union County resulted in significant blowing snow and whiteout conditions across the area. No information was received about injuries from the vehicle accidents.

events.cz_name: MIDDLE RIO GRANDE VALLEY/ALBUQUERQUE METRO AREA
events.event_narrative: With a dangerous fire weather pattern in place across all of northern and central New Mexico due to exceptionally dry conditions and very strong winds, the stage was set for fires to spread quickly. On April 11, 2022, a human-caused wildfire was started northeast of Belen. The Big Hole Fire spread quickly to 890 acres by April 15th with 60 percent containment, and the wildfire was finally 100 percent contained on April 25th. One home was destroyed while eighteen outbuildings were also destroyed, but over one hundred other residences were threatened due to its close proximity to Belen. One firefighter was injured while responding. Damages are estimated.

A barn caught on fire just north of San Antonio on Olguin Road. With very high winds across the area, sparks from the barn fire were carried which started a brush fire. Fortunately, crews were able to contain the fire within about two hours, but the barn as well as one camper were lost. Damages are estimated.

Police officer observed a tornado touching the ground for about two minutes near the Tucumcari airport, moving northeast. The Quay County Sun newspaper reported the tornado between the I-40 frontage road (on the south side) and county road 62, and east of county road AK. No damage was reported from this brief tornado as it crossed open fields.

The McBride Fire started on Tuesday, April 12, 2022, in Gavilan Canyon within the Village of Ruidoso and spread quickly due to 70 to 80 mph winds in the area. By Thursday, April 14th, the fire had burned more than 5,700 acres and burned 207 homes and structures while threatening 1,000 more. The wildfire prompted mandatory evacuations for an estimated 5,000 people. By Sunday, April 17th, the wildfire grew to 6,185 acres, but was 52 percent contained which allowed for evacuation orders to be lifted. At the end of the month on April 30th, the McBride Fire was 95 percent contained. The wildfire is estimated to be fully contained in early May. The cause of the wildfire is unknown. Unfortunately, this wildfire was responsible for the deaths of an elderly couple in Ruidoso. The couple tried to evacuate according to family members, but were unaccounted for. While their vehicle was still at their destroyed home, their remains were found near their home on Wednesday, April 13th. No other information has been made available. Damages are estimated.

events.event_narrative: On April 6, 2022, a prescribed burn was started 12 miles northwest of Las Vegas, but due to windy conditions in place, the fire soon got out of control and spread rapidly. By April 13th, the Hermits Peak Fire grew to 7,900 acres with 10 percent containment. On April 22nd, the wildfire experienced rapid growth as a historic and catastrophic fire weather pattern developed across New Mexico. Despite 91 percent containment, the wildfire experienced rapid growth and combined with the nearby Calf Canyon Fire. Together, these two wildfires burned over 42,000 acres. As very windy conditions persisted through the remainder of April, the Hermits Peak Fire continued to spread rapidly, and by the end of the month on April 30th, the combined acreage between it and the Calf Canyon Fire was 103,908 acres with now 30 percent containment. Currently, the wildfire may not be fully contained until July 2022. Seven outbuildings were destroyed by this wildfire with an additional 600 structures threatened. Mandatory evacuations were not ordered. Damages are estimated.

A downed power line about 4.3 miles southwest of Nogal sparked the Nogal Canyon Fire on April 12, 2022. This fire spread to 400 acres by April 13th and destroyed 6 homes and 8 outbuildings while threatening 50 others. Residences in Nogal Canyon up to New Mexico State Highway 37 were given evacuation orders. By April 17th, the fire had spread to 433 acres with 4 percent containment. By the end of the month on April 30th, the Nogal Canyon Fire was 84 percent contained with full containment anticipated in May. Damages are estimated.

events.cz_name: EAST SLOPES SANGRE DE CRISTO MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: While daily rounds of widespread high fire danger persisted across northern and central New Mexico throughout the month of April, conditions were primed for rapid wildfire growth. The Calf Canyon Fire was sparked on April 19, 2022, near Gallinas Canyon. The wildfire experienced its most rapid growth on April 22nd as a historic and catastrophic fire weather pattern developed across New Mexico. With several hours of widespread 60 to 80 mph wind gusts, the Calf Canyon Fire exploded. This prompted the National Weather Service Albuquerque Office to issue a rare Fire Weather Warning for mandatory evacuations across western San Miguel and Mora counties. By the morning of April 23rd, it was reported that the Calf Canyon Fire had merged with the nearby Hermits Peak Fire, and together, these two fires had burned more than 42,000 acres. A week later, on April 29th, yet another widespread dangerous wind event caused the Calf Canyon and Hermits Peak fires to continue to rapidly spread. This prompted another set of mandatory evacuations across western San Miguel County and the issuance of another rare Fire Weather Warning. By the end of the month of April 30th, the Calf Canyon and Hermits Peak wildfires had burned a combined 103,908 acres with 30 percent containment. The Calf Canyon Fire may not be fully contained until July 2022. Up until this point of the fire season, the Calf Canyon Fire has been the most devastating for New Mexico. It is estimated that many homes and structures have been destroyed as citizens come forward with stories about losing everything they have. However, at this time, there is no estimate on how much has been lost as officials have been unable to do official surveys. Damages are estimated.

events.cz_name: EAST SLOPES SANGRE DE CRISTO MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: On April 17, 2022, the Cooks Peak Fire began on private land north of Ocate near the Mora and Colfax county line. The wildfire experienced its most rapid growth on April 22nd as a historic and catastrophic fire weather pattern set up over New Mexico underneath widespread 60 to 80 mph wind gusts. An infrared flight on the night of April 22nd estimated that the wildfire had grown to 42,672 acres. The rapid growth of this fire prompted evacuations for numerous communities across Mora and Colfax counties. The rapid growth of the wildfire continued through the remainder of the month with a persistent and dangerous windy pattern. By the end of the month on April 30th, the Cooks Peak Fire had burned 59,063 acres with 69 percent containment. Currently, full containment is expected in May 2022.

The Cerro Pelado Fire began during the afternoon hours of April 22nd approximately seven miles east of Jemez Springs. With very high winds in the area, this fire rapidly spread, and by the morning of April 23rd, it had grown to 4,688 acres. Evacuation orders were quickly given for Sierra de Los Pinos and other communities near the Cerro Pelado Fire. This fire even prompted the closure of New Mexico State Road 4 that leads to Los Alamos. Within a matter of days, this wildfire began to move into the burn scar of the 2011 Las Conchas Fire, the 2013 Thompson Ridge Fire, and the 2017 Cajete Fire. As a persistent windy pattern continued through the remainder of the month of April, this fire only rapidly spread. After the next very windy event on April 29th, the fire had spread to 15,650 acres with only 15 percent containment. By the end of the month on April 30th, the fire had burned 17,885 acres with containment now down to 10 percent. Three homes were destroyed by this fire, but no information has been given as to what day those homes were lost. Many other homes and structures remain threatened by this fire. Damages are estimated.

events.event_narrative: The Cooks Peak Fire started on April 17, 2022 on private land north of Ocate. As a persistent windy pattern continued through the month of April, the fire grew rapidly to 59,063 acres. At the start of the month of May, Philmont Scout Ranch Back Country west of New Mexico State Road 21 in Colax County were given mandatory evacuation orders while in Mora County, residents of Los LeFebres, Los Huerros, and residents east of County Road 009 and north of New Mexico Highway 120 were also given evacuation orders. Firefighters were able to make significant progress on the Cooks Peak Fire during the early part of May. By May 3rd, the wildfire was 59,359 acres with 72 percent containment. By May 13th, the wildfire was 100 percent contained with that same acreage. A total of four buildings were destroyed by the Cooks Peak Fire. Ten injuries were reported from firefighting efforts. events.event_narrative: The Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon Fire continued to devastate the area as it grew significantly during the month of May. The wildfire at the end of April was at 103,908 acres, but continued strong winds across the area throughout the month of May allowed the wildfire to spread rapidly. Within the first three days of May, the fire grew over 40,000 acres to a total of 145,854 acres with only 20% containment. During this time, the fire pushed northward toward Mora and northwest toward Las Tusas and Sapello. It also pushed towards Las Vegas, prompting evacuation orders for the western side of the city. By May 16, the Hermits Peak/Calf Canyon Fire grew to 298,060 acres, officially surpassing the 2012 Whitewater-Baldy Fire and becoming the largest wildfire in New Mexico State history. By the end of the month, the wildfire burned 315,627 acres with 50% containment. Official numbers for homes and structures destroyed are still unknown, but on May 17th, the San Miguel County Sherrif reported that at least 340 homes had been destroyed with 275 other structures lost as well. Damages are estimated.

The Cerro Pelado Fire, which began in April 2022, continued to grow rapidly during the month of May. At the end of April, the wildfire had grown to 17,885 acres, and as a very windy pattern persisted during May, this acreage grew quickly. Within the first ten days of the month of May, the Cerro Pelado Fire grew to 42,491 acres. This wildfire prompted the closures of the nearby Bandelier National Monument and the Valles Caldera National Preserve. By the end of the month of May, the wildfire grew to 45,605 acres with 95 percent containment. Currently, no known structures were burned during May.

events.event_narrative: As the largest wildfire in New Mexico State history, the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon Fire continued to devastate the area as it continued to grow. The good news for firefighting efforts was the early onset of the monsoon. Beneficial rainfall impacted the area as early as mid-June, helping firefighters and emergency personnel with containment. By the end of May, the wildfire had burned 315,627 acres with 50% containment. By the end of June, the wildfire had burned 341,735 acres with 93% containment. Full containment of this fire is anticipated in July.

The Cerro Pelado Fire, which began in April 2022 and grew rapidly during the month of May, was finally contained by June 15th. The wildfire burned 45,605 acres during this time. No known structures were burned during June.

The Cerro Bandera Fire began on June 9th on private land within the El Malpais National Monument. Dry and windy conditions allowed this fire to spread to 939 acres before it was contained on June 16th. Four structures, including one home, were destroyed. No other information was given. Damages are estimated.

The Sixty-Six Fire was first reported on June 16th off of Interstate 40 in Carnuel. Dry and windy conditions allowed the fire to spread to 26 acres before it was fully contained on June 21st. Unfortnately, one home, two outbuildings, and one power pole were burned or significantly damaged. No other information was provided. Damages are estimated.

Rainfall totals of 2 to 3 inches across southern portions of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar caused significant flash flooding and debris flow. Widespread flooding was observed along Highway 105 with drainages well out of their banks. A barn along Highway 105 was also flooded. This forced the closure of the highway for several hours on July 1st. County Road A4B was also flooded with debris flow across the roadway. Damages are estimated.

Damages are estimated.

New Mexico Department of Transportation personnel worked through the overnight hours to clear the roadways and reopen them. An estimated 1 to 1.5 inches of heavy rain on the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar flooded New Mexico State Road 434, forcing the closure of the roadway. Near Guadalupita, a residential driveway turned into a raging river with deep water and debris. Canoncito Creek also flooded which was caused by debris caught in culverts. The creek overflowed into nearby pastures, onto Highway 518, and impacted homes within the area. The water was two feet deep in some locations. Damages are estimated.
Highway 60 was flooded at mile marker 31 and State Road 601 was flooded between mile markers 2 and 4.  One house was flooded in Quemado.
State Road 434 was closed between mile markers 6 and 13 due to flooding.

Manuelitas Creek rose four to five feet and overtopped two bridges along County Road A1 east of State Road 94 between Sapello and Manuelitas. One CoCoRaHS observer near Sapello measured 3.76 inches of rain and remarked that it was the highest flooding levels they had seen in their 58 years at that residence. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain in the Santa Fe area caused the arroyos to fill up, and unfortunately, one man was found dead in the arroyo near Cerrillos and Rodeo. According to the Santa Fe emergency manager, the flooding within the arroyo was thought to be a contributing factor to the individual's death. However, the man also sustained blunt force trauma to the head and was also intoxicated, and these factors also contributed to his death. His age is unknown.

A trained spotter traveling on Interstate 40 near mile marker 286 near Santa Rosa reported that strong winds overturned a semi-truck. This was likely due to a microburst, and the nearby Santa Rosa AWOS was only reporting winds of 17 mph at the time of the accident. There was no information on injuries. Damages are estimated for the semi-truck.

Heavy rain on the McBride burn scar caused flash flooding and debris flow within Gavilan Canyon. Photos shared by the Lincoln County emergency manager shows mud and debris across Gavilan Canyon Road which made the roadway impassable. Photos shared also depicted significant flooding and debris flow at the Gavilan Canyon Hideaway and Escape RV Park with mud and debris making roadways impassable. Damages are estimated.
A trained spotter near Clovis estimated a 60 mph wind gust associated with thunderstorm outflow. No damage was reported.
An ASOS station near Gallup measured a 58 mph wind gust likely associated with strong downburst winds.
An estimated 60 mph thunderstorm gust was observed near Red Hill likely from strong downburst winds.

Heavy rain on the northern portion of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar caused significant flash flooding near Holman. Video obtained by KRQE showed fast moving water near residences in Holman, and this flooding also washed out Highway 518. Canoncito Creek overflowed again as well, creating deep water below homes and destroying a number of pastures. Damages are estimated.

An estimated one to two inches of rain across the northern portion of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar in Mora County. This caused significant flash flooding across the burn scar with Highway 518 and the Holman area hit particularly hard. Highway 518 was washed out from near the Taos County line to Cleveland. Video obtained from multiple broadcast media sources showed fast moving water and debris flow impacting numerous residences in Holman, Chacon, and Cleveland. Canoncito Creek was had major overflow with water flowing onto pastures, around homes, across area roadways, and one spotter remarked that it created a lake in some places. Damages are estimated.

Training thunderstorms across the southern portion of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar in San Miguel County produced an estimated 2 to 4 inches of rainfall within the Tecolote Creek and Gallinas Creek areas which caused significant and catastropic flash flooding. Flash flooding and debris flow washed out many roadways within the area, rendering them impassable. The camp director at the Camp Blue Haven said that their playground was underwater for about 40 minutes until water receded. At 2:40 PM MDT, the chief of the Cabo Lucero Volunteer Fire Department received a call about a vehicle floating within the flood waters. When officials responded to the floating vehicle, they also discovered two people dead nearby. While initially thought to have been in their vehicle, officials later determined that the two women, 62-year-old Linda June Cummings and 84-year-old Betty Greenhaw, were swept away from a destroyed home within the Tecolote Canyon subdivision. A third individual from the same home was reported missing, and the National Guard, New Mexico State Police, and San Miguel County Sheriff's Office assised in search and rescue for several days. Finally on Tuesday, July 26th, they found the body of 62-year-old Jimmy Chris Cummings. All three were from Hale Center, Texas, but had a 100-year-lease on a cabin in Tecolote Canyon on the Camp Blue Haven property which they were visiting at the time. Eight feet of water rushing down into the canyon took down two walls of the cabin and partially destroyed the other two walls. Damages for this event are estimated.

Heavy rain on the northern end of the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar caused flooding on the Canoncito Creek. This washed out roads, destroyed pastures, and inundated homes. Damages are estimated.

A heavy thunderstorm over the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon burn scar early in the day on July 23rd dropped between 0.50 and 0.75 inches of rain. This prompted a Flash Flood Warning for the burn scar, however, no reports of flooding were received. The water from this thunderstorm was held back thanks to debris flow. Around midnight, the New Mexico State EOC relayed reports of major flooding and debris flow from a light shower that was only producing a couple hundredths of an inch. This light rain was enough to release the heavier rain that had fallen earlier that day which washed out roads and impacted the Holman area. Damages are estimated.

The Lincoln County emergency manager reported flash flooding and debris flow from the McBride burn scar at Gavilan Canyon and Warrior Drive. This forced the closure of the roadway. Local law enforcement remarked that this flooding was worse than the event on July 20th. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain near Alamo caused flash flooding along New Mexico State Road 169 and mile marker 29. Damages are estimated.

Forest thinning in the Magdalena Mountains resulted in a flash flooding event that made it easier for water to rush down an unnamed canyon. Floodwaters left behind a pile of debris 6 feet high and 20 feet wide that included steel fence posts and barbed wire, damaged trailed, and boulders that were 200 to 300 pounds. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain in the Flora Vista to Bloomfield area in San Juan County caused significant flash flooding in the area. A spotter reported that approximately two feet of water covered County Road 3150, rendering it impassable. Two vehicles were washed away and one home was flooded. Near Crouch Mesa, the San Juan emergency manager reported flash flooding over area roadways, and an RV was washed out. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain resulted in water over Highway 217 near Greenridge Boulevard. No damages were noted.

Heavy rain of 2 to 3 inches near Lamy and Glorieta caused flash flooding in the area. A CoCoRaHS observer reported that this heavy rain flooded the arroyo in their backyard, forming a lake. Video shared by local broadcast media also showed flash flooding through a property at La Posta Way. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain in the Tesuque and Chupadero areas resulted in flash flooding. North-northwest of Tesuque, an arroyo overflowed its banks and flooded a backyard near the intersection of Tesuque Village Road and Highway 592. Flash flooding and mud flow also trapped 15 cars in a Tesuque market. Near Chupadero, the emergency manager reported that water over Rio En Medio Road in six locations along roadway. Damages are estimated.

An Army representative working at the ICP on the Calf Canyon Fire reported that Gallinas Creek overflowed its banks by two to three feet. No damage was reported. Note: Previously, this fire had been referred to as the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon Fire. Officials have remained this fire the Calf Canyon Fire, therefore, from here on out, it will be referred to as such.

Flash flooding was observed on the northern portion of the Calf Canyon burn scar as heavy rain estimated at 0.75 inches to 1.5 inches fell. The Rito de Gascon rose about four feet and overtopped its banks. Nearby, raging flood waters were observed along a road near Monte Aplanado. The problematic Canoncito Creek also overtopped its banks again which flooded roads and pastures and destroyed fences. Damages are estimated.
Video shared by local broadcast media on Twitter showed flash flooding and mud flow along County Road 117S in Nambe. There are no known damages.

A COOP observer near Pedernal reported minor roof damage to an old school building in Encino. According to a friend of theirs, they reported that a tornado or landspout impacted the northeast corner of the building. However, with no picture of the supposed tornado or supporting velocity radar data, this could not be confirmed. Time is estimated based on radar data. Damages are also estimated.
A COOP observer near Encino measured 1.75 inches of rain from a heavy thunderstorm. This resulted in flash flooding near their property. Time is estimated based on radar. No damage was reported.
Video shared by local broadcast media shows raging water in a rural part of Pojoaque. Time is estimated based on radar data. No damage reported.

Video shared by local broadcast media showed a haboob approaching Shiprock, likely generated from strong downburst winds from nearby thunderstorms. While the nearby Farmington ASOS reported thunderstorms, it never reported any visibility restrictions.

Heavy rain estimated at 1 to 1.5 inches caused major flooding on the northern portion of the Calf Canyon burn scar. The Gascon and Cleveland areas were hardest hit again as they have been for most of the month of July. In Gascon, fast moving water carried logs and boulders downstream, and Highway 105 near Camp Davis was flooded. A spotter remarked that four waterfalls were rushing down Gascon Peak. Near Cleveland, signficant flooding was reported along the Rio la Casa with boulders flowing downstream. At least two bridges were flooded, including one on Highway 518. Also near Cleveland, the Canoncito Creek overflowed its banks again, flooding pastures and several properties along the creek. Highway 518 was flooded along this creek as well. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain in the Church Rock and Fort Wingate areas caused flash flooding along Interstate 40 and New Mexico State Highway 118 as reported by the New Mexico Department of Transportation. There are no known damages.
A trained spotter near Logan reported quarter size hail. The hail did damage to tree leaves and destroyed their garden. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused the Rito San Jose to overflow its banks and flood low water crossings along County Road A4 near Rociada. No damages were reported.
Heavy rain across the Calf Canyon burn scar caused the Manuelitas Creek to overflow its banks and flood low water crossings along County Road A1. No damages were reported.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flash flooding and debris flow with a rock slide on County Road 65 near the E.V. Campground. Three people were rescued from flooding in this area. Damages are estimated.
A video shared via Facebook showed flash flooding in the Gallup area. Area and timing is estimated via radar as video was made unavailable shortly after it was shared. No damages are known.
Heavy rain in the Manuelito area forced the closure of New Mexico State Highway 118 at mile marker 11 in both directions due to flooding. No damages are known.

Heavy rain in the Rio Rancho and Vista Hills areas caused flooding. At a home in Rio Rancho, standing water was reported two inches deep in someone's backyard. In Vista Hills, dirt roads were flooded and arroyos were reported to be running. Damages are estimated.
A trained spotter near Edgewood reported that their home was inundated with water from flash flooding. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain of 3.5 to 4 inches caused flash flooding south of Clayton. A trained spotter reported that the heavy rain caused Carrizo Creek to overflow its banks. Standing water and debris was reported across area roadways and within fields. Damages are estimated.
A trained spotter near San Fidel reported flash flooding on San Jose Loop. No damages are known.
Heavy rain northwest of Magdalena caused flash flooding along New Mexico State Road 169 at mile marker 9.8, forcing the closure of the roadway. No damages are known.
Heavy rain on the Rito de Gascon within the Calf Canyon burn scar caused it to overflow its banks and cause debris and ash flow within the area. No damages are known.
Heavy rain near Santa Clara Pueblo caused the Santa Clara Creek to overflow its banks and cause flash flooding in the area. No damage was reported.

events.cz_name: EAST SLOPES SANGRE DE CRISTO MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: At the end of June 2022, the largest wildfire in New Mexico State history had burned 341,735 acres with 93% containment. Containment on the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon Fire was anticipated in July, but the western edge of the wildfire was within very steep terrain that was inaccessible to first responders. Thus, progress on this wildfire slowed down during the month of July. Fortunately, a very active month for monsoon season brought much needed moisture to the fire, and containment rose to 96% with no change in the acreage burned. No known structures were lost during the month. Note: While originally known as the Hermits Peak and Calf Canyon Fire, officials renamed the fire to the Calf Canyon Fire on July 26, 2022. Moving forward, this is how the wildfire will be referred.

A COOP observer near Villanueva reported dime to quarter size hail from a thunderstorm.
A COOP observer near Villanueva reported that the heavy rain caused flooding with water over roadways within the village. No damage was reported.
A member of the public reported that the intersection of Spring Drive SE and Black Hills Road SE near Cabezon was underwater from fast flowing flood waters. No damages were reported.
Heavy rain caused 4 to 6 inches of fast moving water to impact the intersection of Frost and Broken Arrow near Sedillo. No damages were reported.
A report of 1.63 inches of heavy rain within one hour on the Calf Canyon burn scar flooded New Mexico State Road 105 near Gascon. No damages were known.
Heavy rain in Chacon near the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flooding across Highway 121. No damages were known.
The Lincoln County emergency manager reported flash flooding on Gavilan Ridge within the McBride burn scar that forced road crews to clean up debris on area roadways. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flash flooding in and around Rociada. Heaviest rains drained into Capulin Canyon flowing to the Rito San Jose and San Jose Church. Video shared on Twitter showed flood waters approaching homes, but exact damages are unknown. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar produced flash flooding in Rociada. Video shared by localy broadcast media showed fast moving debris flow overrunning property and structures. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain in the Tajique area caused flash flooding along New Mexico State Road 55, rendering it impassable as crews worked to clear water and debris off the roadway. No damages were known.
Heavy rain near Navajo washed out Service Road 9452 as water flowed out of the arroyo due to debris caught in the drainage. Damages are estimated. Time is estimated based on radar.

Heavy rain near Mexican Springs flooded Service Road 30. The emergency manager reported that several areas of the roadway were damaged to the flooding. Damages are estimated. Time is estimated based on radar.

Heavy rain over the Calf Canyon burn scar during the afternoon drained towards the Las Vegas area through the evening hours. An inebriated motorcyclist attempted to cross a flooded low water crossing at Gallinas Creek and El Llano Road in Las Vegas, but had to be rescued when they failed. Any potential injuries to the motorcyclist are unknown. Timing of this event is a rough estimate given radar. Damages are estimated.

Flash flooding on the Calf Canyon burn scar led to flash flooding and debris flow in the Holman area. A couple of homes near New Mexico State Road 518 one half mile south of State Road 121 were impacted by the flood waters, and water was reported over the roadway in some spots. Signifcant flooding was also reported on Canoncito and Encinal Creeks, endangering property and destroying pastures. County Road B-022 was flooded all the way across State Road 518 to the Mora River. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar led to flash flooding and debris flow in the Cleveland area. Flash flooding was reported along New Mexico State Road 518 with flood waters very close to nearby homes. Damages are estimated.

A reporter for the Santa Fe New Mexican relayed reports of flash flooding on the Medio burn scar. A large work truck was found destroyed from the flood waters, and large boulders and trees were moved and found in the streambed. The date of this event was not clear, and thus date and timing is a rough estimate based on radar. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar drained into Montezuma, flooding New Mexico State Road 65 and forcing the closure of the roadway at mile marker 4. Damages are not known.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flash flooding on Highway 434 near El Turquillo. A vehicle containing the 30-year-old driver John Vasquez and a 64-year-old passenger Benjamin Torres attempted to cross the flooded roadway, but were unsuccessful as the vehicle was caught in the flood waters. Vasquez was able to escape through an open car window with only minor injuries, but Torres remained trapped in the vehicle. Once the flood waters receded, first responders discovered Torres deceased in the vehicle 100 yards downstream. Vasquez was arrested and charged with vehicular homicide while under the influence of alcohol and fleeing an accident with knowledge of death or great bodily harm. Damages are estimated for the loss of the vehicle.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused flooding along Highway 105 and Highway 276. This forced the closure of Highway 105 at mile marker 5 and the closure of Highway 276 at mile marker 0. Damages are estimated.

A rock slide on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused by heavy rainfall impacted New Mexico State Highway 121 from mile markers 3 to 5. This forced the closure of the roadway and trapped vehicles on the road. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused debris flow along New Mexico State Highway 518, rendering the roadway impassable near Holman. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the McBride burn scar caused flash flooding along Gavilan Canyon Road near the intersection of Eagle Creek Canyon Road in Ruidoso. Damages are estimated.

Heavy rain near Golden caused flash flooding on Puertocito Road, forcing the closure of the roadway with debris and large boulders rendering it unpassable. Time of the report is estimated based on radar. Damages are estimated.
Hail covered interstate 25 near mile marker 379. Highway crews had to use plows to remove the hail from the interstate.
Flooding along the Rio Bonito dislodged a couple of foot bridges at the Lincoln State Monument and moved them downstream approximately one eighth of a mile.

Flash flooding struck the northeast part of Santa Fe. Arroyos became torrents and overflowed their banks in some instances. Major street flooding ensued in some locations, especially along Lorenzo Road which saw mud deposited two feet deep. One man drowned when he was swept down an arroyo. An unoccupied automobile was damaged when it was also swept down an arroyo. Flash flooding occurred at the Morales Bridge on the north side of town, and a home was flooded on Circle Dr nearby.
Video shared by local broadcast media showed flooding and debris flow on the Cerro Pelado burn scar near Sierra de Los Pinos and the East Fork Jemez River. No damages are known.

A rock slide was reported along Highway 68 between Taos and Embudo. This rock slide was likely caused by repeated rounds of rainfall and not just this one event. Exact time of the rock slide is unknown and is estimated from radar. Damages are estimated.
The IMET on the Calf Canyon fire reported flash flooding along New Mexico 276 due to the Maestas Creek overfilling its banks. Damages are not known.
Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused Canoncito Creek to overfill its banks and flood Highway 518. Damages are not known.

Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar ran into the Rito San Jose, causing it to overfill its banks. This caused significant flooding near Rociada as high and fast-moving water ran up against a house near Highway 105 and County Road A4B. Water nearly swept away a large propane tank as well. Reports were also received of water near another building in Rociada and with water up to the bumpers of several parks vehicles. Damages are a rough estimate.

The Colfax County emergency manager reported minor damage to State Route 21 as the nearby Moras Creek and Rayado Creek flowed over the roadway. Damage was mainly along the shoulder. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain near Church Rock forced the closure of Interstate 40 in both directions at mile marker 33.

Video shared on the social media platform Tik Tok showed impressive and devastating flash flooding near Sheep Springs. A massive wave of water near U.S. Highway 491 swept horse trailers, farm equipment, and lawn furniture downstream. Water overtopped the hoods of parked vehicles and inundated a few structures and residences. Damages are a rough estimate.
Heavy rain near Tse Bonito caused water to flow over State Route 264 at mile marker 1. Reports were received of cars stalled on the roadway. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain near Yah-Ta-Hey caused water to flow over State Route 264 at mile markers 9 through 10. Any damages are not known.
Heavy rain on the McBride burn scar caused flash flooding along Gavilan Canyon Road, near Warrior Drive. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the Calf Canyon burn scar caused water and debris to overtop a bridge along Highway 266 at the Sapello River. Damages are estimated.

The San Juan County emergency manager reported flash flooding at Chaco National Park. High water rises were reported along the Chaco River, and one unknown roadway within the park was completely destroyed. Time of this report is estimated based on radar, and damages are also estimated.
Flash flooding reported along County Road 4990 at Armenta Wash near Bloomfield with water flowing over the roadway. This completely destroyed the roadway. Damages are estimated.
Heavy rain on the McBride burn scar caused water and debris to flow over Devil's Canyon Road at an Eagle Creek low water crossing. Damagers were not known.

The Lincoln County emergency manager reported that hours of light, steady rainfall with totals of 1 to 2.5 inches caused burn scar flash flooding on the McBride burn scar near Ruidoso. All of Gavilan Canyon was flooded. Damages are estimated.

Consistent rainfall near Mesa caused flooding along U.S. Highway 285 which stranded motorists between mile markers 144 and 146. Water rescues were also needed at mile marker 139. The extent of damages are not known and are estimated for the stranded vehicles.

events.cz_name: EAST SLOPES SANGRE DE CRISTO MOUNTAINS
events.event_narrative: New Mexico's largest wildfire in state history was finally 100% contained on August 21, 2022 after burning for four months. The Calf Canyon fire burned 341,735 acres on the east slopes of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, northwest of Las Vegas. No damages from the wildfire were known during the month of August.
Heavy rain in the Cuba area caused flooding over U.S. Highway 550 which impeded traffic. No damages are known.
Heavy rain in eastern Albuquerque caused street flooding across portions of the metro area. No damages are known.

Localized heavy rain near Taos clogged an arroyo, causing water to flood the Los Cordovas area. Blueberry Hill Road at Lower Las Colonias Road was closed due to flash flooding with water two feet in depth. Two nearby houses had about one foot of standing water inside. New Mexico Highway 240 near Cotton Road was also closed due to four feet of water over the roadway. Damages are estimated.
Brief heavy rain near El Rancho caused the arroyos to run, and a truck somehow got stuck within the arroyo.

A long duration rain event across the area caused the Pecos River to swell to record values. The Acme gauge, located to the northeast of Roswell along the river, entered action stage during the early morning hours of August 21st, and water levels continued to rise quickly to a crest of 17.37 feet by about 2 PM MDT. This was well over the major flood stage of 16 feet, and it set a new record for the Acme gauge. The gauge stayed in major flood stage for about seven hours before gradually falling below action stage during the evening hours of August 22nd. This record flooding along the Pecos River caused major impacts in the area. Near Bitter Lake National Wildlife Refuge, the Chaves County emergency manager relayed reports of a truck that was stuck within the flood waters with the driver having to be rescued. Damages are estimated.

A long duration rain event caused the Pecos River in Chaves County to swell and cause major flooding around the river. Once the Acme gauge to the northeast of Roswell crested to major flood stage, that water slowly traveled south for several days, causing flooding in the Dexter, Hagerman, and Lake Arthur areas. The gauge at Lake Arthur crested to a maximum of 13.37 feet at about 6:45 PM MDT on August 26th. Despite this being well below action stage, major impacts were still felt for several days across southern Chaves County along the Pecos River. During the early morning hours of the 21st, a vehicle attempting to cross a flooded low water crossing was carried about a half mile downstream along Cherokee Road near Hagerman. A water rescue was conducted for the driver who was found sitting on the top of their partially submerged vehicle. Along River Road at Bottomless Lakes, four people had to be rescued. Two of these individuals were rescued from a trapped vehicle while the other two were rescued from the home after they previously chose not to evacuate. Finally, near Dexter, three people had to be rescued from their vehicle. This water rescue proved to be particularly difficult as the flood waters at this point were too high which prevented emergency officials from reaching the stranded travelers. Officials had to drive around Dexter and approach the location from the east to rescue the three individuals. Despite all this, there were no known injuries and damages are a rough estimate.
One person was rescued from the flooded Embudo Diversion Channel near Interstate 40 and Carlisle Avenue.
The sheriffs dispatch reported state road 117 was washed out near the El Malpais Ranger Station.
Half dollar size hail was reported east of Yeso.

An ASOS station in Farmington measured a brief wind gust of 58 mph due to strong downburst winds from nearby showers and thunderstorms.
Thunderstorm outflow winds caused a 65 mph wind gust at a public weather station near Golden.
Thunderstorm outflow winds caused a 67 mph wind gust measured by a public weather station near Stanley.

A nearly stationary thunderstorm over El Porvenir produced over two inches of rainfall on this area of the Calf Canyon burn scar. This caused flash flooding on Beaver Creek and Gallinas Creek with significant debris found on Highway 65. The IMET on duty found several locations along Highway 65 that were covered in tree debris, rocks, and mud. Some buildings along the roadway were inundated with a couple of feet of water. The IMET also noted that water had threatened homes in the area as well, but these homes seemed to have been protected with sandbagging. Damages are estimated.

Localized heavy rainfall on Gavilan Ridge flowed downhill onto the McBride burn scar which caused flash flooding along Gavilan Canyon Road from Janet Drive northward to Airplane Canyon. Burn scar flash flooding resulted in rock and mud debris along the roadway. Damages are estimated.
An ASOS station near Roswell briefly measured a 58 mph wind gust from strong downburst winds.

Widespread, serious flooding occurred from the upper canyon of the Rio Ruidoso downstream through the towns of Ruidoso, Hollywood and Ruidoso Downs as far east as Fox Caves. Flooding also occurred along the Rio Bonito from the dam at Bonito Lake downstream to State Road 48.  Flooding was extensive in Ruidoso, not only along the Rio Ruidoso, Cedar Creek and other small streams, but also throughout the town from the 6 to 7 inches of rainfall that fell there. One man was killed when we was swept away by the raging Rio Ruidoso, but no other substantial injuries were reported. A total of 500 structures, including campers and mobile homes were damaged. Around 200 houses were damaged, and some were completely destroyed. At least 13 bridges were washed out and several cars were washed downstream. Several dozen recreational vehicles and campers were damaged at an RV park at Ruidoso Downs.

The Blue 2 wildfire was discovered a few days after it's lightning caused initiation on May 16th within the old Little Bear burn scar. It began in a remote area of the White Mountain Wilderness just southwest of Bonito Lake and west of the village of Ruidoso. After an initial size of 45 acres, the Blue 2 fire grew quickly to 1,478 acres on May 24th due critical fire weather conditions highlighted by dry, windy, warm and unstable weather. Evacuations were put in place for Bonito Lake with shelters opened at the Lincoln County Fairgrounds as a result from the fire growth on May 24th, that expanded to the Villa Madonna Subdivision on the 25th. Red flag conditions allowed the fire to grow to 7,455 acres through May 25th. Some small containment up to 5 percent was finally accomplished on the fire by the end of the month. Thus far, no damage or loss of life has been reported.

Cloud to ground lightning started the Indios wildfire in a remote area of the Chama River Canyon 7 miles north of the village of Coyote, NM on May 19th. The wildfire burned through the remote wilderness growing in size to 450 acres by the 21st. Critical fire weather conditions on May 24th and 25th allowed the fire to rapidly grow in size to 1,809 acres on the 24th and to 2,619 through the 25th. The fire grew to 8,733 acres by the end of the month with 25 percent containment. No damage or loss of life has been reported with this fire.

High winds along and behind an outflow boundary from storms west of Roswell resulted in blowing dust across southern Chaves County. Visibility at the Roswell Air Center dropped to a quarter mile at 15:35 MDT due to the blowing dust. The low visibility from the blowing dust resulted in multiple vehicle crashes on the Roswell Relief Route between Sunset and Brasher Road, U.S. Highway 285 from mile marker 99 to 112, and State Road 2 from mile marker 4 to 6 resulting in the closure of the highways. Two vehicle pileups were observed on U.S. Highway 285 west of Dexter and Hagerman, one near the intersection of Ojibwa Road and another near the intersection of Orchard Park Road. Winds tapered off shortly after 17:00 MDT allowing the dust to settle and visibility to improve.

Multiple photos and a video were shared on Twitter/X showing a well defined landspout beneath a strong thunderstorm cell just northwest of Crownpoint, NM. The video clearly shows the landspout north to northeast of the intersection of Navajo Service Route 89 and Navajo Service Route 9. Subsequent photos and radar support the track of the landspout moving east toward NM Highway 371 north of Crownpoint. No damage was reported and is not surprising given the extremely remote location. Location and track are based on the combination of analysis of the photos, video and radar data.

The South Fork Fire was discovered on June 17th within tribal land along the Rio Ruidoso west of Ruidoso. It blew up in size within its first two days reaching 15,000 acres and destroying an estimated 1,400 structures. Two lives were lost, an as of yet identified person in a vehicle on Rainier Road due to the limited remains, and a 60 year old Patrick Pearson within the Swiss Chalet Motel. The fire's growth slowed considerably by the 19th due to heavy rainfall causing flash flooding on the burn scar. Flash flooding and debris flows exacerbated recovery efforts. Many of the structures lost were located within the eastern and northeastern portion of the burn area including areas from Alto to Cellars Canyon and Cedar Canyon down to the upper Rio Ruidoso. Damage is an estimate based on number of structures destroyed.

events.event_narrative: Strong outflow winds from thunderstorms along the central mountain chain resulted in a haboob moving west across Interstate 25. The lower visibility resulted in a 23 car pile up and the resultant closure of Interstate 25 between San Felipe casino and Santo Domingo Pueblo. News reports showed 51 people were taken to the hospital.

Multiple areas of water and hail across NM 161 with debris flow making the highway impassable. Field and drainage flooding was also reported.
Underpass to I-25 Exit 361 flooded with rapidly rushing water and widespread flooding in the fields along the interstate. That road was covered with several inches of small hail.
Accumulated hail up to quarters in size was embedded within flash flooding over I-25 near and just south of Watrous.
NM 542 just north of the intersection with NM 55 closed due to heavy rains and 8 to 10 inches of fast flowing water over the highway.

Flash flooding and debris flow within the eastern edge of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar resulted in a bridge being washed out along County Road A3. Exact location is unknown and damage is an estimate.
A trained spotter reported debris including trees and mud coming down the mountain from intense storms. Timing is an estimate based on radar.

Flooding over U.S. Highway 85 at mile markers 200 and 204 requiring debris removal. Reports of home damage from arroyo flooding, and a water rescue of a couple trapped in a mobile home due to surrounding flood waters. Injuries are unknown. Flood damage reported in homes from the arroyo flooding. Damage costs are an estimate.

Heavy rains forced sharp rises along the Rio Chama between Medanales and Espanola. These rises were observed to peak at 7.95 feet at the Rio Chama near Chamita (CMTN5) gauge, resulting in flooding along U.S. Highway 84 between the junction of U.S. Highway 285 and Abiquiu that impacted 40 residences. This also resulted in heavy sand deposits near Medanales that resulted in the Rio Chama rerouting through adjacent agricultural fields two days later on June 22nd. Damage is an estimate given the lack of information and is an aggregate of the damage caused by the rerouting of the Rio Chama into the aforementioned agricultural fields as this was a direct result of the flash flooding that occurred on the night of the 20th into the morning of the 21st.
The Gallup Airport measured a peak thunderstorm wind gust of 60 mph.
Widespread flooding reported along Tecolote Creek in Mineral Hill stretching over to NM Highway 283 from mile markers 3 to 13 that closed the highway. Any damage is unknown.

Flash flooding from heavy rains closed NM Highway 65 from mile markers 2 to 4 or one mile south of Montezuma where culverts were washed out. Flowing water 1 to 3 feet deep also reported over El Llano Road, Cinder Road, Palo Verde Road and at the intersection of 7th Street and Mills Avenue. Road closures were also reported along State Road 65 at Campus and El Camino, as well as along 8th Street north of Mills Avenue. Robertson Cardinal football field was completely covered in standing water. The Las Vegas Water Treatment Plant also flooded. A mandatory evacuation order was issued at 9:54pm MDT for this area due to the dangerous flooding across Las Vegas to Montezuma. Damage is an estimated given very limited information.
Quarter to golf ball size hail reported just southwest of Bloomfield.
Power lines reported down along Old Aztec Highway (County Road 3520) between Penny Lane and Lake Luther. Damage is an estimate.
A member of the public estimated 70 to 80 mph wind gusts.
A single wide mobile home was pushed off its blocks with minor damage to the structure. Damage is an estimate.

A trained spotter measured a 65 mph wind gust. A single wide mobile home was pushed off its blocks with minor damage to the structure. Other wind damage reports include a tree limb falling through a roof, a mangled metal car port, damaged horse sheds, and 15 power poles blown down. Damage is an estimate.

Multiple reports of flash flooding across Farmington including along the La Plata and San Juan Rivers, including vehicles driving across flooded low water crossings. A video from the emergency manager showed the La Plata River raging and partly out of its banks. These included along Southside River Road on the west side of Farmington. A vehicle was stuck in a ditch along the San Juan River, thankfully the driver made it out safely. There was an overflowing ditch and arroyo with fast moving water at Brookside Drive and Navajo Street. There was several inches of water moving across Crouch Mesa east of Farmington and south of Flora Vista. U.S. Highway 64 at Andrea Drive and between County Road 5500 and 5777 where the road was completely flooded with swift moving water and impassable. A normally dry wash also observed a one foot rise with debris including small pieces of furniture. Flooding lasted well after the heavy rains ended as evident on the San Juan River gauge (FRMN5) showing river levels did not recede until after 10:00 pm MDT. Damage is an estimate based on the very limited information provided.

The Cibola County Emergency manager reported multiple vehicle rescues from flood waters. The Rio San Jose was out of its banks between Sargent and Davis Streets with several streets flooded in town. Swift moving water several inches deep was observed over First Street and Roosevelt Avenue. Damage is an estimate.

Heavy rain on the McBride burn scar resulted in flash flooding with mud and ash off the hillsides roughly between NM 48 and Eagle Creek Road, and a second area along Gavilan Canyon road by Meander Drive was washed out with debris over the roadway. Both sections of Gavilan Canyon Road were closed. A water main break also occurred that exacerbated the situation. Damage is an estimate based on clearing the debris on the roadway.

Raging waters on Cedar Creek overtopped its banks in spots, resulting in the closure of Paradise Canyon Road near Hull Road. Muskat Ball Drive at Cedar Creek was impassable due to flooding with medium to heavy debris. County Road 127A (Upper Eagle Creek Road) was impassible with medium to heavy debris along the road. Alto Lake also flooded over a short time.

Heavy rains over the new South Fork burn scar resulted in flash flooding along Cedar Creek that raged through the Innsbrook Village near NM Highway 48. An NWS Employee also recorded flash flooding along Cedar Creek down to Paradise Canyon Drive. Damage is unknown, and may be more related to the South Fork Wildfire.
The Encerrita Wildfire was a lightning start discovered within the El Malpais National Monument. The fire burned a total of 2,499 acres resulting in no damage or loss of life.

The Antone Wildfire located within the Gallo and Mangas Mountains south of Quemado in Catron County was a lightning start wildfire. The fire was managed and allowed to grow to a final size of 12,397 acres. There was no damage to property or loss of life.

Multiple reports of a landspout, possibly multiple landspouts just east of Hagerman were collected and relayed by the Hagerman Police Chief. A poorly constructed and dilapidated trailer home was destroyed by this landspout. Time is estimated based on a corresponding wind gust measurement and radar data. Path is also based on the multiple reports on the east side of Hagerman likely aligning up to be the one landspout that tracked northward.

Multiple reports of a landspout, or landspouts were relayed by the Hagerman Police Chief on the west side of town. This landspout was reported to have begun on the southwest side of town reaching the RV Park at Argyle Street and Wichita Road. No damage was attributed to this individual landspout. Timing is based on limited radar data.

A peak wind gust of 91mph was reported by a trained spotter near Hagerman. Corresponding thunderstorm wind damage as relayed by the police chief and the Roswell Daily News included a barn and pivot on Morgan Road, a portion of a metal roof being torn off from a residence, and 40 to 50 electric poles and 8 transmission lines. There were several reports of fallen trees in town as well, including one at the Hagerman Public Schools. The Chaves County Undersheriff also reported a road closure along U.S. Highway 285 between mile markers 83 and 90 due to traffic accidences induced by low visibility brownout conditions. Thankfully, there were no reports of injuries or fatalities. Damage is an estimate.

Lightning struck a tree in the front yard of a residence at 207 Linden Street in Hagerman, NM. The large and very alive tree was split down its main trunk with large branches causing damage to the roof of the house and their vehicle.
The Cannon AFB weather station measured a peak gust of 63 mph.
A NMDOT mesonet station along I-40 at State Road 6 measured a peak thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph.
The Gallup Airport weather station measured a peak thunderstorm gust o 63mph.
Water flooding over NM 605 north of Milan prompted the closure of the highway.

NMDOT reported the bridge along U.S. Highway 64 at the AZ border was severely damaged by flash flooding. The original bridge was in the process of being replaced and what was destroyed was a temporary bridge structure until a new bridge was constructed. Damage is an estimate.

Flash flooding and a debris flow was reported in Eagle Creek within the new South Fork burn area crossing NM Highway 532 (Ski Run Road) between mile markers 2 and 3. This debris flow was reported to have reached the Alto Reservoir, overtopping the diversion channel. The Cow Mountain RAWS near the headwaters of Eagle Creek recorded 1.48 inches of total rainfall this day. Damage from this individual event is unknown. However, there were more impactful debris flows and flash flooding within the South Fork burn scar further south and through Ruidoso.

Heavy rain totaling 1.48 inches at the Cow Mountain RAWS station and radar estimated to be higher than 2 inches over the recent South Fork burn scar produced life threatening and extremely dangerous debris flows down Cedar Creek just north of Ruidoso. This torrent raged through town overtopping several bridges and crossings including, Mechem Road (NM Highway 48), Paradise Canyon Road, Cree Meadows Road, and Wiley Road. The debris flow also overtopped a small dam near Cree Meadows Road. Fire crews were pulled out of sensitive areas due to the threat of heavy rains and an evacuation order was issued for the Village of Ruidoso just after 4pm MDT. Some people became trapped in their vehicle along Paradise Canyon Road, requiring swift water rescue. This one swift water rescue was one of a total of 26 swift water rescues for the day caused by the flash flooding and debris flow that occurred across the Village of Ruidoso. Miraculously, there were no reports of injuries or fatalities. Damage is an estimate based on cars and road crossings being involved.

Heavy rains over the recent South Fork burn area totaling up to 1.48 inches at the Cow Mountain RAWS and estimate by radar to have surpassed 2 inches caused flash flooding heavy debris flows along the Rio Ruidoso. This torrent impacted several bridges and water crossings including, N. Eagle Drive, Grindstone Canyon Road, Country Club Drive. Numerous homes were impacted with a total of 26 swift water rescues stretched across the Rio Ruidoso and Cedar Creek drainages through the Village of Ruidoso. Fire crews were pulled out of sensitive areas due to the threat of heavy rains and an evacuation order was issued for the Village of Ruidoso shortly after 4pm MDT. The debris flow eventually reached downstream past the Village of Ruidoso to the Ruidoso Downs Track overtopping the edge of the facility and flowing out over the track. For reference, the Ruidoso Downs Track was constructed over the Rio Ruidoso. Miraculously there were no reports of injuries or fatalities. Damage is an estimate based extent and limited information.
Water and debris completely covered Gavilan Canyon Road at the Gavilan Canyon Softball Field, making the road impassable.
The Albuquerque Sunport measured a peak thunderstorms wind gust of 72mph.
A public report of three inch tree limbs broken and power poles down.
NMDOT reported standing water on NM 542 and NM 55 prompting a road closure.

Heavy rain measured to have ranged from 1 to 2 inches within one hour across the Albuquerque metro area caused major flash flooding. Underpasses and low lying intersections in downtown were inundated with deep floodwaters. An SUV and public transit bus were partially submerged under the water and had to be retrieved by a tow truck. There were reports of street flooding and vehicles being stranded elsewhere across town. The Albuquerque Fire Department reported they performed 7 swift water rescues in the arroyos around town and 18 overall responses to folks impacted by the floodwaters. Of these responses, 10 were to help people stranded. An unknown number of homes near downtown and south of downtown received flood damage. The Albuquerque Police Department, Convention Center and City Hall also experienced flooding, but the damage was mostly aesthetic according to media reports. Total damage is an estimate based on limited information and extent of damage.
A NMDOT mesonet station along I-25 at La Bajada measured a peak thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph.
Heavy rains overnight produced flash flooding along NM-65 just north and northwest of Las Vegas, NM. There were no reports of damage.

Heavy rains on the Hermit's Peak Calf Canyon burn scar resulted in flash flooding and water over the highway at multiple points of State Road 283 just west of Las Vegas, NM. There were no reports of damage.

Severe thunderstorm winds destroyed two out-buildings, one large wooden barn and one steel metal shop in Quemado, NM. The steel building ended up landing on top of the neighbors residence and caused significant damage to the structure. There were no reports of injuries.

Slow moving storms developed over the burn scars near Ruidoso with an estimated 4 to 6 inches of rainfall on the eastern half of the Salt burn scar. Flash flooding and debris flow raged down drainages along U.S. Highway 70 to the Ruidoso Hospital and intersection with Sudderth Road. The NM National Guard reported conducting 45 swift water rescues through the day and early evening, including an unknown number at the Rainbow Lake RV Park on Carrizozo Canyon Road. Roads were also impassable at Brady Canyon Rd., Porr Dr., Leon Farrar Dr., University Dr. and Mechem Dr., among others. Video was captured of the torrent of flood waters and debris flow sweeping a dumpster and multiple vehicles down U.S. Highway 70, including a semi-truck. An evacuation was ordered for the Upper Canyon area of Ruidoso. Miraculously, there were no reports of injury or fatalities. Damage is an estimate.
Outflow from approaching thunderstorms produced a 59 mph wind gust at the Belen Regional Airport.
Nearby thunderstorms resulted in a peak wind gust of 68 mph at the Mine Mesonet on the White Sands Missile Range.
A trained spotter in Los Alamos reported nickel size hail from a thunderstorm.
A thunderstorm produced a microburst at the Raton Crews Airport resulting in a peak wind gust of 59 mph.
A severe thunderstorm dropped ping pong size hail a few miles south of Raton along Interstate 25.
A severe thunderstorm produced hail up to golf ball size and a peak wind gust of 60 mph in Rainsville.
A public spotter reported golf ball size hail from a severe thunderstorm a few miles east northeast of Glencoe.
A cooperative observer a mile south southeast of Dilia observed quarter size hail from a severe thunderstorm.
An observer at Tecolotito observed quarter size hail from a severe thunderstorm.
The Dunken mesonet station observed a peak wind gust of 65 mph from a severe thunderstorm.
A very brief and ragged tornado touched down in the rural countryside of San Miguel County north of Las Vegas and Interstate 25. No damage was observed.
A trained spotter a few miles near Ranchville reported half inch to penny size hail from a brief strong thunderstorm.
A trained spotter in Portair along U.S Highway 60 and 84 just north of Cannon Air Force Base observed quarter size hail from a severe thunderstorm.
A peak wind gust of 62 mph was observed at Cannon AFB from nearby thunderstorms.
A public spotter reported quarter size hail from a severe thunderstorm a few miles east of Ute Park.
A cooperative observer near Fenton Lake State Park in the Jemez Mountains observed penny size hail from a strong thunderstorm.
A public spotter observed nickel size hail near San Ysidro from a strong thunderstorm.
Flash flooding occurred in Las Vegas on Mills Avenue near the state Behavior Health Institute Building.

Heavy rainfall from thunderstorms on the South Fork and Salt Fire burn scars resulted in flash flooding and debris flows across the Upper Canyon and Brady Canyon neighborhoods along the Rio Ruidoso. A bridge on Main Road at McDaniel Road was washed from the debris flow and runoff. Video on social media showed the roof of a house along with other household debris sliding down the Rio Ruidoso upper canyon among fast moving water. Additionally, a woman was trapped in a tree due to high rushing water. Runoff from the rainfall moved downstream through the Rio Ruidoso exceeding its banks and impacting the Fern Trail and Paradise Canyon near downtown Ruidoso. Several car and water rescues were conducted in this area. The Riverside RV Park in Hollywood along the banks of the Rio Ruidoso was completely flooded out. Another video on social media showed the Rio Ruidoso at Ruidoso Downs Racetrack and Casino out of its banks flooding the horse racetrack. Additionally, crews with excavators are seen digging up dirt along the banks of the Rio Ruidoso at the racetrack cleaning up prior flash flood damage. Thankfully, no injuries or fatalities were reported from the catastrophic flash flooding. Property damage cost is an estimate.
The Ruidoso emergency manager forwarded a video of a landspout in the Upper Canyon area. The time, length and width of landspout estimated based on derived radar products and video footage.

Multiple rounds of heavy rainfall from thunderstorms impacted the South Fork and Salt Fire burn scars for a second day in a row. This resulted in exacerbated flash flooding and debris flow in the same locations along the Rio Ruidoso. A house near downtown Ruidoso was reported to have been pushed 10 feet due to flash flooding. A busted water line and gas leak were also reported in the area. An SUV with 3 occupants inside floated down the Rio Ruidoso. Thankfully, all 3 occupants were rescued. The worst impacts from this episode of flash flooding and debris flow occurred on U.S. Highway 70 in Hollywood. The highway and its various intersections, including Mechem Drive and Sudderth Drive were shut down. Fast and heavy debris flow resulted in a road collapse near the Sudderth Dr. and U.S. Highway 70 intersection. The debris flowing down U.S. Highway 70 at one point included a large shipping container. Property damage cost is an estimate.
A severe thunderstorm dropped quarter size hail in Ute Park.
A trained spotter reported 1 inch hail in Chamizal from a severe thunderstorm.
A mesonet at Dunken measured a wind gust of 68 mph from nearby thunderstorms.
The Little Burro mesonet on the White Sand Missile Range observed a peak wind gust of 64 mph from nearby thunderstorms.
Thunderstorm outflow winds partially removed the roof of a residence in Little Water, New Mexico. Time estimated based on limited radar data. Property damage cost estimated.
Severe drought remained across the eastern portion of the zone.

The Fisher Wildfire was a lightning started wildfire discovered within the San Mateo Mountains of western Socorro County. The fire was managed by the Magdalena Ranger District allowing it to grow to 8043 acres. No damage was reported.
The Ridge Wildfire started in the Gila National Forest in southern Catron County reaching a total size of 4,257 acres. Little to no damage was reported outside of closures along trails.
The lightning caused Yeso Wildfire was discovered near the Mesa del Yeso in eastern Rio Arriba County. The fire was managed and allowed to grow to 650 acres causing no damage.
The lightning caused Mestenas Canyon Wildfire was located roughly 12 miles southwest of Dulce along U.S. Highway 64. The fire grew to 837 acres reaching its containment lines by July 25th.
The lightning caused Lolo Wildfire was located near Escondido Mountain six miles northeast of Quemado Lake. The fire was managed and caused little to no impacts, growing to 438 acres.
Flash flooding occurred along Bonito Canyon and other small drainages southeast of Corona.
Flash flooding occurred near Ancho.  A fence near a home was taken down by the flowing water.  Rainfall was measured at 2.76 inches.
NMDOT reported difficulty driving on NM Highway 50 between mile markers 1 and 3 due to standing water and debris over the roadway.
A radio report of flash flooding was received from heavy rain on the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar along NM Highway 94 just north and west of Sapello, NM.
KOB relayed a viewer report of flash flooding on NM Highway 50 near exit 299 near Glorieta, NM. There was a foot of water over the roadway.
Trained spotter reported 3 inch tree limbs snapped from tree. No damage was reported.
WSM40 Mine White Sands Missile Range recorded a 63mph thunderstorm wind gust.
The Tucumcari Airport recorded a 58mph thunderstorm wind gust.

A late evening batch of moderate to heavy showers passed over the complex of burn scars in and around Ruidoso producing a half inch to one inch of rainfall in the area. Catastrophic flash flooding occurred, focusing through Cedar Creek and the Rio Ruidoso after 11pm MDT. Flood waters overtopping bridges and roadways were reported in several areas including Mechem Dr. at Brady Canyon Dr., U.S. Highway 70 at Cedar Creek, and Paradise Canyon Road at Cedar Creek. Evacuations were ordered from the Upper Canyon area to areas along the Rio Ruidoso from west of town through to mobile home areas near Hollywood along U.S. Highway 70. Several swift water rescues were conducted, including for two vehicles trapped in water near Johnson Rd., an elderly resident who was unable to evacuate on Brady Canyon Dr., and one resident trapped on one side of a bridge at Paradise Rd. and Foothill Rd. that was overtopped by water. Cherokee Mobile Home Park sustained damage with water flowing beneath mobile homes. Home damage was reported along Brady Canyon Dr. from the elderly couple who needed assistance evacuating. A culvert on Cedar Creek above the ranger station was completely torn out and washed out onto the roadway. Rises on the Rio Ruidoso at the Hollywood gage spiked from 1.58 feet to 8.16 feet within 90 minutes before waters started to recede.

Heavy thunderstorms on the South Fork burn scar resulted in another round of burn scar flash flooding, debris flow and severe property damage across the Upper Canyon and Brady Canyon neighborhoods along Mechem Drive west of downtown Ruidoso. Bridge 2 at Main Road and Fox Road became impassible due to flooding. Debris flows resulted in arching powerlines over the flood water at Brady Canyon. An SUV was trapped against a tree due to flood waters just north of Brady Canyon Road. There was a rescue of two juveniles from a house at Meander Drive and Paradise Canyon Drive. Runoff from the flash flooding resulted in the Rio Ruidoso to instantly rise to major flood stage and a new record level of 15.80 feet. This resulted in more flash flooding at the Ruidoso Downs Casino horse racetrack. Flash flooding caused damage to the racetrack, two bridges near the entrance of the facility, and in the barn area. After this latest instance of flash flooding, officials decided to shut down the horse racetrack for the remainder of the summer season and move upcoming scheduled races to Albuquerque. Thankfully, no injuries or fatalities were reported from this instance of burn scar flash flooding. Property damage is an estimate.

Tijeras Arroyo overtopped Via Sedillo for the second time in a week. The large embankment created by road crews to protect the roadway from additional flood waters was blown out again. Mud, rocks, and debris covered a large section of the roadway.
A cluster of thunderstorms produced a 58 mph wind gust at the Albuquerque Sunport.
The Sevilleta mesonet station recorded a 59 mph wind gust from thunderstorm outflow. Time estimated based on radar reflectivity.
The Phillips Hill White Sands Missile Range mesonet station recorded peak wind gusts of 62 mph from thunderstorms moving through the site.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms resulted in flash flooding with a depth of 6 inches across parts of Portales. Locations included U.S. 70 and Kilgore Road in northeast Portales and 18th Street near downtown Portales. No reports of any damage from flooding.

Rainfall amounts of around half an inch over the South Fork burn scar resulted in more flash flooding across the Upper Canyon and Brady Canyon neighborhoods west of downtown Ruidoso. Runoff on the burn scar resulted in flash flooding on the Rio Ruidoso resulting in road closures along and near the banks of the river, including White Mountain and Sunny Slope Drive, Brady Canyon Road and Mechem from Cedar Creek, and Gavilan Canyon Road. Property damage is an estimate.
NM DOT reported flooding on mile marker 7 along NM 434 which prompted a road closure and the deployment of a cleanup crew to clear rocks and debris.
Heavy rain caused an already full retention pond at the Roswell Country Club to overflow.  Water seeped into three nearby homes.
Emergency manager reported Brady Canyon Dr. and Ponderosa Dr. were closed due to water flowing over the roadway, caused by burn scar flash flooding.

Rainfall amounts of 0.50 to 1.50 inches fell on the South Fork burn scar west of downtown Ruidoso during the early afternoon hours. This rainfall resulted in more burn scar flash flooding and debris flows across neighborhoods in Alto and Ruidoso. The Cherokee Mobile Village along U.S. Highway 70 at the Lincoln and Otero County line was evacuated due to flash flooding. Mechem Dr. became impassible again due to Cedar Creek overflowing its banks and rushing over the roadway. Heavy flows along Cedar Creek caused Mechem Dr. to become impassable, washed out a part of Musket Ball Dr. and brought debris flow over Cree Meadows Drive. Flooding of the Rio Ruidoso resulted in the closure of Gavilan Canyon Road and the evacuation of the Gavilan Mobile Home Park. Debris flow on the Rio Ruidoso destroyed a culvert on the eastern end of the Ruidoso Downs racetrack. Water and debris flow reported west of Alto making NM 532 impassable. Fortunately, no reports of significant water rises were received downstream of the water breach at Ruidoso Downs. Culvert and trailer park damage cost is an estimate.
A lightning start wildfire 27 miles north of Cuba that was managed to 5,800 acres.
A COOP observer reported quarter size hail at Pasamonte, NM.
Large live tree snapped and damaged utility power lines at 2nd and Main Street in Clayton, NM.
The Clayton Airport measured a peak wind gust of 63mph.

Flash flooding and debris flows on the Rio Ruidoso in the Upper Canyon area along Main Road was relayed by Emergency Management and was seen on a USGS camera. Debris piled up and clogged some culverts along Main Road in Ruidoso. Another debris flow from this same heavy rain event resulted in the closure of Gavilan Canyon Bridge near Hollywood. Overall, the debris flows stayed within the banks of the Rio Ruidoso and did not overwhelm any of the main bridges in Ruidoso. Damage cost is an estimate based on cleanup costs of the clogged culverts.
The Melrose Gunnery Range station recorded a peak wind gust of 72 mph and sustained winds of 53 mph from a wet microburst.
The local Fire Department reported flooding near the junction of Alpine Village Road and NM Highway 48 just south of Alto, NM.
Local law enforcement reported flash flooding just outside of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon burn scar along NM 434 at mile marker 3 that closed the road.
The Clovis Municipal Airport AWOS measured a peak thunderstorm wind gust of 58 mph.
Cannon AFB weather reported spotty flooding with 8 to 12 inches depth of water in spots, but no impassable streets.
